title: The economy: a wave moving through time

steps.title: From the universe to an economy
steps.text: The blue level ends in nations. Here one of them, the United States, opens into its economy, and the same cause-and-effect logic continues: like the food chain, every business feeds on the layers beneath it, down to the government it all stands on. From here, up means money: market value for firms, income rank for people.
steps.reading: At now the road of lives fans out into the economy's wave.
steps.measured: UN age pyramids; US marriage, divorce and birth rates
steps.assumed: each line is a simulated life standing for many people
steps.caption: the United States stream → its economy

steps.title: A wave moving through time
steps.text: The road of American lives since 1950 and the economy's accounts since 1946 share one time axis. At now, the cross-section opens into a wave: each rib behind the crest is one year, widening as real output grows. The crest is the year shown, and the past recedes behind it. This is a model, built on public accounts and on assumptions.
steps.reading: Width grows with the square root of real output: 11 times the output since 1947 draws the industries about 3.3 times as wide; the gaps between tiers stay fixed.
steps.measured: real output and the national accounts (BEA)
steps.assumed: the wave's shape and its square-root width

steps.title: The bedrock: government
steps.text: Government is the bedrock everything stands on. In the United States it is a constitutional federal democracy. Its pillars are sized by public outlays; taxes fall into it from every household, and benefits rise out of it.
steps.reading: Pillars rise out of the bedrock to the people they pay.
steps.measured: federal, state and local outlays and taxes (OMB, BEA)
steps.judged: how regulated each industry is, and how much it shapes its own rules
steps.assumed: government drawn as the layer everything stands on

steps.title: The price of money
steps.text: The state reaches into every market through two levers: the price of money, which the central bank sets and every debt pays, and the edge of trade. Money was dearest in 1981, at 16.4% a year, and nearly free from 2009 to 2016. Tariffs fell from 7% of the value of imported goods in 1947 to under 2% in the 2010s, then tripled in 2025, from 2.6% to 8.0%.
steps.reading: Height is percent a year; time runs left to right, 1947 to now.
steps.measured: Federal Reserve, Freddie Mac and Treasury rates; customs duties and imports (BEA)

steps.title: What if: the US economy on another government
steps.text: A thought experiment: the same American hills on other states' foundations. The bedrock is as deep as what each state spends: 38% of GDP in the United States, 49% in Sweden, 33% in China, 29% in Saudi Arabia, 48% in the Soviet Union of 1980. Summits turn steel where the state controls the largest firm: in China the largest bank, oil company, power grid and telephone company, while private firms lead technology and retail. Saudi Arabia's state lives on oil: 60% of its revenue. In the Soviet Union every summit belonged to the state.
steps.reading: The view steps through the five states in the card's order.
steps.measured: state spending and revenue (IMF), its stakes in the largest firms, trade, elections
steps.judged: each state's rules and the firms that shape them
steps.assumed: another state's foundation under the US hills; each summit is its industry's largest firm

steps.title: Layers standing on layers
steps.text: On the bedrock, layers stand on layers: raw materials and subsistence infrastructure at the foot, then manufacturing and infrastructure, then services, with technology on top. Each industry is a ridge as wide as its share of value added. Height here is an order of dependence, not of importance.
steps.reading: Width is each industry's share of value added; height is the assumed order of dependence, not measured value.

steps.title: Companies live and die
steps.text: 75 companies live on the ridges like people on the road: born, rising and falling with market value, then failing, bought, or reaching the crest. Their color shows how they sell: meeting needs, manufactured want, or fear.
steps.reading: Height above a ridge is market value on a compressed scale: a $3 trillion company stands 2.3 times as tall as a $10 billion one.
steps.measured: market values, births and fates of 75 companies
steps.judged: how each company sells: to needs, wants or fears

steps.title: Companies spend too
steps.text: Companies run the same program as people. A firm's year of money leaves in the directions it flows: down to its suppliers and workers, forward into the future as investment, split between desire for new demand and fear of falling behind, up to its owners, and into the state as taxes and lobbying. Arrows show which way the money moves it. In 2025 five companies spent $449 billion on capital, about two-thirds of it judged to be for artificial intelligence, and it poured down the hill.
steps.reading: White arrows: which way the money moves the firm, as Jev judged it.
steps.judged: investment's desire and fear, its AI share, which way the money moves each firm
steps.assumed: each firm's split between suppliers and workers, from its industry's accounts

steps.title: Golden circles
steps.text: At every market the dollar splits: wages run back down to workers, taxes fall to the bedrock, and the surplus climbs to gold halos above the summits and to the rings of owners around the top firms - the golden circles.

key.label: rings that pay more than they collect

steps.reading: Of each household dollar in 2025, before income taxes, the model gives wages about 41¢, owners 27¢ and sales and property taxes 7¢; upkeep and imports take the rest.
steps.measured: how each industry's dollar splits (BEA input-output accounts)
steps.assumed: who owns each firm: the top 1%'s share of all stock times the firm's value (two rings name real owners)

steps.title: Attention above capital
steps.text: Above the capital float the most followed Americans, ringed by how many of the other most-followed follow them. Attention runs in a loop: companies pay the platforms $295 billion a year in digital advertising, the platforms and brands pay creators about $37 billion, people give about two hours a day and take in wants, and then they spend.

key.label: the loop: attention given, then money spent

steps.reading: Size is followers; position in the cloud is who follows whom, not rank.
steps.measured: followers and follows; US digital advertising (IAB) and creator spending
steps.assumed: the widths of the loop's attention and spending legs

steps.title: Class is height on the hill that pays you
steps.text: Class is altitude. People live on the slope of whatever pays them, as close as possible to their source of value: an employer's industry, the government, or family wealth. The out of work sit on the valley floor; the richest float above.
steps.reading: Altitude is the rung on the hill that pays you; across hills, height is the industry's assumed tier.
steps.measured: national income and wealth totals the simulated people are calibrated to
steps.assumed: the tiers' heights and class as altitude

steps.title: Rivers of desire and fear
steps.text: Money flows in two colors: desire, in rose, and fear, in ice. Spending runs down to each industry's market; saving leaves over the crest into the future, and debt arrives from it.
steps.reading: A river widens with the money spent through it in a year.
steps.judged: whether each kind of purchase serves a desire or a fear
steps.assumed: each spending category's stored share of fear

steps.title: Who moved up or down, and what came with it
steps.text: The hill's altitude pulled out beside the wave: five rungs of household income in 2015 and in 2025, joined by streams of people. Among adults 25 to 54, a lost job, a divorce and unpayable debt came with the falls; work, a child, a home and marriage with the climbs. These are associations in the simulation, not causes. Counted as the tax records count people, adults 25 and older, the model's bottom fifth holds its members about as tightly as the Treasury's records, where 55% stay a decade; the dots by the bottom and top rungs set the two side by side.
steps.reading: Streams are simulated adults, calibrated to national totals; their width is people.
steps.measured: the benchmarks: the Treasury's tax panel and the PSID survey
steps.assumed: the simulated lives and what comes with their moves

steps.title: One person
steps.text: Zoom into a single person. Where they stand on this hillside is where they stand in the social market: the slope that pays them, the rung they occupy, and the people around them. They are synthetic: each stands in for many real people.
steps.reading: The figure stands on its household's hill, at the rung of its income.
steps.assumed: a synthetic person who stands for 100,000 people, and their drives

steps.title: Inside one mind
steps.text: Inside one mind: five desire drives and five fear drives, weighed by reason into a choice. Desire pulls toward the hills that pay and please; fear pushes away from debt, loss and scarcity. It is a simplified mind: its drives are a group's average, and their weights are assumptions.

key.label: memory: what is owned and owed

steps.reading: Each drive's size is its share of the motive; reason weighs them into spending and saving.
steps.assumed: the drives' weights and how reason weighs them

steps.title: Tit for tat
steps.text: Every encounter is a prisoner's dilemma: cooperate or defect. Tit-for-tat opens kindly, copies the partner's last move, retaliates and forgives. Over many rounds the payoffs add up; the dollars they add here are illustrative.
steps.reading: Each pulse between two seats is a move in one round.
steps.assumed: the strategies, the payoffs and their worth in dollars

steps.title: Groups play the same game
steps.text: Groups play the same game as people: cooperation, retaliation and forgiveness between groups and tribes. Coalitions form where cooperation keeps paying, and break where it does not. These are model experiments, not forecasts.
steps.reading: Two rings, two tribes: 128 groups of people play tit for tat within and across them.
steps.assumed: the groups' strategies and the season's rules

steps.title: The ladder
steps.text: One life's path across the landscape over time, climbing and falling between rungs, compared with the parents' rung. Job changes, marriage, children and debt move it up or down.
steps.reading: Each year stands at its place on the road, on the rung of that year's household income.
steps.assumed: a synthetic life: its events and what they cost

steps.title: Where do you stand?
steps.text: Tell the model about your household in the panel. It places you among the year's simulated Americans: your rung on the hill you work on, where each dollar you spend goes, how much of everyone's income goes to people ranked above you, how far you are from living on what you own, and where people like you were ten years later. Nothing you enter is kept. It is a mirror, not a forecast.

key.label: income that goes to people ranked above you

steps.reading: Beside you, on a ruler of the income fifths: where people like you were ten years later, a step for each fifth they reached, each ribbon as wide as its share. The tour waits while you try it.
steps.measured: the national totals the simulated people are calibrated to
steps.assumed: the simulated population; that your spending pays people the way everyone's does; a 4% yield for living on what you own

steps.title: Somewhere on this hillside
steps.text: Back to the whole wave. It is a model, with assumptions built into it, but its shape follows everything before it: the economy is the newest layer of the same causal chain that began with the Big Bang - and you are somewhere on this hillside, moving with it into the future.
steps.reading: The past recedes behind the crest; ahead of it lies the future, not yet made.
